title: Work with me
text: I am Tanmay Chanda, a data scientist and R and Shiny developer. I build production Shiny applications, and I maintain three R packages on CRAN.

title: Work with me
text:
What I can help with
Production Shiny apps. I build modular Shiny apps with golem, for real users. This includes data import and validation, interactive tables and dashboards, Docker, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, deployment to Azure, and unit and end-to-end tests.
Shiny that people must trust. Some apps are in regulated or audit-heavy settings, where users must trust the numbers. I build audit trails, validation rules, and reconciliation and de-duplication of data from many sources. I also show users where a result came from.
Shiny performance and UX. I find slow reactives, add loading states, and give users undo and redo.
Bayesian marketing mix models and forecasts. I build Bayesian MMM and forecasts in R with brms. I have 3+ years of experience with media budgets for large US clients.
Workshops and talks. I give hands-on sessions on production Shiny, on testing Shiny apps, and on Shiny in regulated settings.

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
text:
Shiny has bookmarking. It has reactlog. It has no undo.
That is strange when you stop to think about it. Undo is in every text editor, every drawing program, every spreadsheet. People arrive at a dashboard already expecting Ctrl+Z to work. Then they change a filter by mistake, and there is no way back except to remember what the filter used to say.
I wrote rewind to close that gap. It is on CRAN now.
Ctrl+Z now steps backwards through the choices the user made. Ctrl+Shift+Z and Ctrl+Y step forwards. There is a pair of buttons and a clickable history rail if you want them.
The package itself is small. The interesting part is not the feature. It is the three problems you meet when you try to build it, and I think each one is worth reading about even if you never install this.

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
section: Problem one: restoring a widget you have never heard of

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
text:
Problem two: the echo
Here is the failure mode that kills most attempts at this.
Restoring an input sends the value to the browser. The browser sets the widget. The widget reports the new value back to the server. The server sees an input change, and records a new history entry.
That is a loop. Undo creates a history entry, which you can then undo, which creates another entry.
Two mechanisms stop it, and they overlap on purpose.
Dedup. The history refuses to accept a state identical to the current one. A restore moves the pointer to state S before the echo arrives, so when the echo turns up it matches the present exactly and is dropped. This handles the common case with no coordination at all.
An expectation guard. The controller remembers what it asked the browser to apply, and ignores intermediate states until either the echo matches or a timeout expires. This covers the case dedup misses: several inputs arriving in separate flushes, producing a half-applied state that is not identical to anything.
Neither depends on guessing how long the round trip takes. That is what makes it reliable rather than usually-correct.

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
section: Problem three: a bug that only R could give you

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
section: The practical bit: one drag is one step
text:
The practical bit: one drag is one step
Dragging a slider fires dozens of input events. Undoing them one at a time would be useless, so changes that land within coalesce_ms of each other become a single entry. One drag is one undo step, not forty.
When time is the wrong boundary - a “reset filters” button that changes four inputs at once - you can say so:
observeEvent(input$reset, {
  rewind_step(label = "Reset filters", {
    updateSelectInput(session, "region", selected = "All")
    updateSliderInput(session, "year", value = c(2018, 2026))
    updateCheckboxInput(session, "active_only", value = FALSE)
  })
})
One entry, with a label a human wrote.
State you keep yourself is invisible until you register it:
state <- reactiveValues(pinned = character(0))
rewind_track(state, fields = "pinned")
Modules work: call rewind_enable() once at the top level and inputs inside modules are captured under their namespaced names and restored correctly.

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
text:
What undo does not do
Undo restores state. It does not undo side effects. If an observer wrote to a database when the filter changed, stepping back changes the filter, not the database row. That is worth being clear about before you put this in front of users who might assume otherwise.

title: Undo for Shiny, and the three problems that make it interesting
text:
Try it
install.packages("rewind")
shiny::runApp(system.file("examples/demo", package = "rewind"))

Documentation: https://tenmeh.github.io/rewind/
Source: https://github.com/tenmeh/rewind
CRAN: https://cran.r-project.org/package=rewind

Issues and pull requests are welcome. I am especially interested in reports from anyone running it inside a heavily modularised app, since that is where the interesting edge cases will be.

title: Where did this number come from?
text:
It started with a box count.
A friend sells plants online. It is a small shop: she takes the photos, answers the emails, and packs every order herself. Last spring I built her a small Shiny dashboard over a weekend. It showed orders, revenue and the best sellers for each month.
A few weeks later she sent me a screenshot. The dashboard said 412 orders for April. Under it she had written: “I packed more than 600 boxes.”
The number was not wrong. I knew that before I looked. The pipeline under it removed test orders, then refunds, then orders that were never paid, and then it cut the month at midnight in UTC, not in her time zone. Each step was right. Together, they made a number that she did not recognise.
So I opened R and ran the pipeline one step at a time. I counted the rows after each step and wrote the counts in a message:
She read it and replied: “OK, that makes sense. Can the dashboard tell me that?”
It could not. That question became whence.

title: Where did this number come from?
text:
The question every dashboard gets
Every dashboard I have built has met some version of it. Someone looks at a number and expects a different one. They do not doubt the arithmetic. They want to know what was left out.
The person who asks is usually not the person who wrote the code. They cannot read the pipeline. Even if they could, a row count is not in the code. It only exists when the code runs.
whence puts the answer next to the number. The viewer clicks it, and a panel opens:
$4,281,330

  Where the rows went
    sales                 18,442 rows
      region == "APAC"     3,180 rows   -15,262 rows (83%)
      year >= 2023         1,204 rows    -1,976 rows (62%)
      aggregated to 1 row      1 row

  Reproduce                                        [Copy]
    sales |>
      filter(region == "APAC") |>
      filter(year >= 2023) |>
      summarise(total = sum(revenue))

  [View the rows]
That is an attrition waterfall: each step, the rows that were left after it, and how many it removed. Under it is the code that makes the number again, with the values of the inputs filled in.
In the app, you change two function names and nothing else:
library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(whence)

ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput("region", "Region", c("APAC", "EMEA")),
  whenceOutput("total", label = "Revenue")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$total <- renderWhence(
    sales |>
      filter(region == input$region) |>
      filter(year >= 2023) |>
      summarise(total = sum(revenue)),
    format = scales::label_dollar()
  )
}
whenceOutput() and renderWhence() take the place of textOutput() and renderText(). The pipeline stays as it was. There are also versions for a summary table, where each row explains itself, and for a ‘ggplot2’ plot of one, where each bar does.
Like the grey boxes of bones, it looked like a small idea. Four parts of it were harder than they looked.

title: Where did this number come from?
section: Problem one: the pipe leaves no trace
text:
Problem one: the pipe leaves no trace
To count the rows after each step, whence has to find the steps. With the native pipe, that is harder than it sounds. The pipe is gone by the time R sees the code:
quote(x |> f() |> g())
#> g(f(x))
There is no list of steps, only calls inside calls. So whence knows a list of verbs, such as filter(), mutate(), summarise() and slice_max(). For a call to one of them, the first argument is the data from upstream. whence walks inward from the outer call until it reaches the source, and the steps fall out in order. The magrittr pipe %>% works the same way.
Each step then runs once, in order, in the environment of the render. It reads the same inputs as the whole expression would. That is the same work as running the pipeline in one piece.

title: Where did this number come from?
section: Problem two: a summary is not a loss
text:
Problem two: a summary is not a loss
This one is a question of meaning, not of code. summarise() turns 1,204 rows into one. A plain waterfall would say “-1,203 rows (99.9%)”.
That is true, and it is also wrong. No row was removed. They were all used. A viewer who reads “-99.9%” thinks the step threw almost everything away.
So a summary step is not shown as attrition. The waterfall says “aggregated to 1 row”, and the share is only shown for steps that drop rows.

title: Where did this number come from?
section: Problem three: one row of a table

title: Where did this number come from?
text:
Problem four: which rows
“View the rows” shows the rows of the source that make the value. A click on a removed count shows the rows that the step removed. In the story at the top, that is where the 167 refunds and unpaid orders would be.
This could be slow, so it happens only when the viewer asks. The steps then run again on a copy of the source with a hidden id column, and the ids that survive are the rows that count.
Some steps break that link. After distinct(), pivot_longer(), pivot_wider() or a step that whence does not know, a row of the result is no longer one row of the source. The panel then says so. The waterfall still works, because counts survive any step.

title: Where did this number come from?
text:
Try it
whence 0.1.0 is on CRAN:
install.packages("whence")

shiny::runApp(system.file("examples", "demo", package = "whence"))
The engine also works with no Shiny at all. whence_trace() takes a pipeline and returns the waterfall:
library(dplyr)

whence_trace(
  mtcars |>
    filter(cyl == 4) |>
    filter(mpg > 25) |>
    summarise(mean_hp = mean(hp))
)

Documentation: https://tenmeh.github.io/whence/
Live demo, in your browser: https://tenmeh.github.io/whence/articles/live-demo.html
Source: https://github.com/tenmeh/whence

My friend still opens her dashboard on the first of each month. These days, when a number looks low, she clicks it.

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
text:
Each of my package posts has a short video near the top. A pointer drags a slider, a menu opens, a caption explains the step. It looks like a screen recording.
It is not one. Nothing in the video was filmed. A script asks a web page for its state at 0 ms, then at 33 ms, then at 67 ms, and takes a picture each time. ffmpeg joins the pictures into a video.
This post is about how that works, and why I did it this way.

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
text:
Why not a screen recording
A screen recording records what happened. I wanted to describe what should happen, and then draw it.
A recording has three problems for a demo that I want to keep:

It is never the same twice. The pointer moves at a slightly different speed. A plot takes a little longer to draw. If I record again next month, the video changes in ways I did not ask for.
It needs the real app running. The apps are R. To record them, I need R, the packages, the data, and a window of the right size, all at once.
A small change means a new take. If I change the blog’s font, every video still shows the old one. With a recording, the only fix is to record again by hand.

The app in the video above is a few lines of R:
library(shiny)
library(rewind)

ui <- fluidPage(
  rewind_buttons(),
  selectInput("region", "Region", c("North", "South", "East", "West")),
  sliderInput("year", "Year", 2018, 2026, 2024),
  plotOutput("plot")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  rewind_enable()

  output$plot <- renderPlot(plot_for(input$region, input$year))
}
The video does not run this app. It shows a page that looks like it, and that page is a function of time.

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
section: A scene is a function of time

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
section: Things that move on their own

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
text:
What it gives me
A video of 9 seconds is 270 frames. Each of my three videos is between 140 KB and 210 KB, smaller than most photos on a phone.
The best part came a few days ago. I changed the colours and the font of this blog. The videos had the old caption colour and the old font. I changed two stylesheets and ran one command. All three videos and their posters were recorded again in under a minute, and nothing else in them changed.
On the page, the video is muted and loops, and it plays by itself where the browser allows it. A reader who asks for less motion gets the poster and the play button instead. In the RSS feed, which other sites such as R-bloggers copy, there is no video at all: the feed shows the poster, with a link to the post.

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
text:
The limits
This is not the right tool for every demo.

It is a recreation. The video shows how the package behaves, not the R code running. If the package changes, the scene does not change with it. I have to keep them in step by hand.
A scene takes time to write. The rewind scene is a few hundred lines of HTML and JavaScript. A screen recording takes a minute.
It cannot show real speed. A demo of how fast something is needs the real thing. Here, the scene decides how long everything takes.

If you want the real app on screen, shinytest2 can drive it and take screenshots of it. Then the timing belongs to the app, not to a clock. For a demo that I want to keep, change and record again, the clock wins.

title: Recording Shiny demos frame by frame
text:
Try it
The scenes and the recorder are in the repository of this blog, in the _previews folder. You need Node, Playwright with Chromium, and ffmpeg. Then:
node _previews/record.mjs          # all scenes
node _previews/record.mjs bones    # one scene
If you make a demo this way, I would like to see it.

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
text:
rewind 0.3.0 is on CRAN. I released it on 25 September. If you update from 0.2.0, you also get the changes in 0.2.1, which I released on GitHub only.
My first post was about adding undo to Shiny, and the problems behind it. This release makes the history more useful to read. It also fixes two bugs where the history worked, but the app around it did not.

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
section: What changed, not only which input
text:
What changed, not only which input
The new rewind_diff() tells you what a step changed. A history label such as "region, year" tells you which inputs changed. It does not tell you what they held before, or what they hold now.
I wanted an app to be able to say "North -> South".


A browser recreation. The table compares the first step with the current step using rewind_diff(from = 1).


Inside a server with rewind_enable() already called, this compares two positions in the history:
rewind_diff(from = 1, to = 3)
Suppose position 1 holds region North and year 2024. At position 3, they hold South and 2020. The result has these six columns, in this order:



from
to
name
change
old
new




1
3
region
North -> South
North
South


1
3
year
2024 -> 2020
2024
2020



This table shows the contents of each cell. old and new are list columns, not text columns. The rows are sorted by name, and name holds the input ID, not the label beside the widget.
That choice matters. An input can hold a date range or a multiple selection. A tracked value can hold a whole data frame. Turning every value into text would lose its type and shape. A list column keeps the value itself. change gives a short description for a person to read.
Without arguments, rewind_diff() compares the current position with the one before it. At the first step, it returns no rows. It depends on the history, so an output can follow it:
output$changed <- renderTable({
  rewind_diff()[, c("name", "change")]
})
The video uses rewind_diff(from = 1) instead. Its table grows as inputs move away from the first step. Undo puts the year back, so that row goes away. The table is a comparison of states, not a record of every action.

This is not an audit trail
I put this limit in the documents on purpose. The history lives in the memory of one session. When the session ends, it goes too. Once it passes depth, it drops the oldest entries. A new change after an undo drops the steps in front of the current position.
Those are useful rules for undo. They are poor rules for a record that someone may need to inspect later.
If you need that record, write it as each change occurs and keep it somewhere else. Do not wait until the session ends and try to recover it from the undo history.

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
section: The rail that scrolled the page

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
section: The module that looked half alive
text:
The module that looked half alive
Undo now works when rewind_enable() is called inside moduleServer(). Before the fix, capture worked and the rail filled up. But no button, shortcut or rail click reached that history.
The browser sends three global input IDs: rewind_undo, rewind_redo and rewind_jump. Inside a module, I watched those names through the module’s session. Shiny looked for the namespaced IDs instead. The sender and the observer were talking about different inputs.
The fix reads those controls from the root session. For undo, it is:
root <- session$rootScope()

obs_undo <- shiny::observeEvent(root$input$rewind_undo, ctrl$undo(),
                               ignoreInit = TRUE, domain = session)
Capture still uses the module session. The controls come from the root.
I find this bug useful to remember because the working half hid the broken half. A growing history looked like proof that the setup was right. When JavaScript sends an input ID, check that the R observer reads that exact ID, especially inside a module.

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
text:
The smaller things
A few more changes come with this update:

The rail shows times in the viewer’s own time zone, instead of UTC. The time column of rewind_history() is unchanged.
coalesce_ms, restore_timeout and hold_ms now refuse NA, NaN and Inf, with a message that names the argument. Before this, Inf in coalesce_ms silently stopped all recording.
rewind_diff() refuses a position such as 2.7. It used to truncate it to 2. The message for from is “from must be a single whole number.”
From 0.2.1, rewind_enable() has restore_timeout, in seconds. It sets how long capture waits for the browser to finish a restore. The default is still 2 seconds.
rewind_buttons() has button_class for classes on the buttons. Its class argument still applies to the container. The arrows are now SVG, so their shape does not depend on the browser’s font.
The redo tooltip says “Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y)”. Ctrl+Y already worked; the button now says so.
The fileInput() check tests column types as well as names. A user data frame with the same four names but different types stays in the history. The names are name, size, type and datapath. A frame that matches both the names and the types is still treated as a file input value.

title: rewind 0.3.0: show what changed
text:
Try it
install.packages("rewind")

Documentation: https://tenmeh.github.io/rewind/
Changelog: https://tenmeh.github.io/rewind/news/index.html
Source: https://github.com/tenmeh/rewind

I would especially like to hear how you use the comparisons. Undo can put a value back. Now an app can also tell the user what that step means.

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
text:
bones 0.1.1 is on CRAN. It was published on 16 October. It is my second package on CRAN, after rewind.
bones gives Shiny outputs loading placeholders in the shape of their content. My first post explains the idea. This one is about getting it through review.
I submitted 0.1.0 on 25 September. The automatic pre-tests on Windows and Debian passed with one NOTE: “New submission”. Every first submission gets that note.
On 6 October, a reviewer sent two requests and ended with “Please fix and resubmit.”

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
section: A package name keeps its case
text:
A package name keeps its case
CRAN asks for the names of packages, software and APIs in the Title and Description fields of DESCRIPTION to be in single quotes. I had written 'Shiny'. The package is called shiny. Package names are case sensitive.
The title is now:
Content-Shaped Loading Placeholders for 'shiny' Outputs
Title Case does not apply inside those quotes. The name must keep the case of the package it names.
R CMD check --as-cran passed with 'Shiny' and gave no note about it. The human reviewer caught it. A clean check does not mean that every name in the prose is right.
There was a second place to fix. Roxygen copies the Title and Description into the package help page, man/bones-package.Rd, through the "_PACKAGE" sentinel. Changing DESCRIPTION alone leaves the old text in the help page and the PDF manual. I had to run roxygen again.
This shell command helps with the name check:
grep -oE "'[^']+'" DESCRIPTION | sort -u
It lists every quoted name. Compare each one with the real name, including its case. Then rebuild the help files that copy those fields.

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
section: Give the settings back, also under inst/
text:
Give the settings back, also under inst/
The other request was to restore changes to par(), options() and the working directory in examples, vignettes and demos. The reviewer added “in your inst folder”.
bones has a demo app under inst/examples/demo/. Users can run it with:
shiny::runApp(system.file("examples/demo", package = "bones"))
Its plots changed par() inside renderPlot() and never put the settings back. R CMD check did not catch this either. The reviewer read inst/ by hand.
The fix saves the old settings and restores them when the function exits:
old_par <- par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0), las = 1)
on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)
on.exit() works inside a renderPlot() expression because Shiny makes that expression the body of a function. The cleanup belongs to that function, and also runs if it exits with an error.
A demo ships with the package too. I need to treat its changes to the user’s settings with the same care as changes in R/.

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
section: Search beyond the line in the reply
text:
Search beyond the line in the reply
The reviewer gave me an example, not a full list. Before resubmitting, I searched the whole package for the same kind of change:
grep -rnE "options\(|par\(|setwd\(|Sys\.setenv\(" R man inst vignettes demo
The demo was the only place. But fixing only the named line would have left me guessing about the rest. That is my first lesson from this release: turn a review comment into a search for the pattern.
I fixed both requests and resubmitted as 0.1.1 on 6 October. A resubmission needs a higher version. The covering comment starts with a “Resubmission” section that lists each change.
Then it waited in CRAN’s folder for new packages, called “newbies”. I could watch the queue at CRAN incoming and on cransays.
On 16 October, the reply was “Thanks, on its way to CRAN.” bones 0.1.1 was published that day.

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
text:
The release that tags itself
My second lesson is to let the GitHub release follow CRAN. A merge is too early. CRAN can still send that version back. GitHub could then show “Latest” beside a version CRAN never published. That nearly happened with 0.1.0.
A workflow in .github/workflows/release.yaml, first written for rewind, runs once a day. It reads the bones version in the CRAN index. If that version has no git tag, it downloads the CRAN tarball.
It finds the oldest commit on main with that version in DESCRIPTION whose files match the tarball. It skips DESCRIPTION, MD5 and build/, which R CMD build and CRAN change. It tags that commit and makes a GitHub release, using that version’s section of NEWS.md as the notes.
On 17 October, it tagged v0.1.1 at the commit sent to CRAN. Main had already moved on. Nobody had to remember to tag it.
Before a package reaches CRAN, the daily run stops with a notice instead of an error. It does not send an email every day.

title: bones is on CRAN: two things the review caught
text:
What comes next
These changes are in the development version for 0.2.0. They are not on CRAN yet:

An error panel when an output fails, in place of Shiny’s red error text.
Learned shapes. After a load, the browser stores the content’s shape, using numbers only, with no text. The next visit shows a skeleton in that shape.
Clear errors for a misspelt shape. type = "bars" says Did you mean "bar"?.

text:

Live demo, in the browser: https://tenmeh.github.io/bones/articles/live-demo.html
Source: https://github.com/tenmeh/bones

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
It started with a reel.
It was one of those short videos that explain a trick of the web. When a page loads, the site does not show you a spinner. It shows you grey boxes in the shape of the page: a bar where the title will be, a rectangle where the picture will be, three lines where the text will be. Then the real content fills in.
The point of the video was that this is a kind of trick. The page is not faster. The data takes as long to arrive as before. But the wait feels shorter, because you already see the shape of what is coming. Your eye goes to the place where the title will be. You start to read the page before there is anything on it.
These grey boxes are called skeleton screens. Once you know about them, you see them everywhere: in social media feeds, in video sites, in almost every large web application.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
Does Shiny have this?
My first thought was about Shiny. A Shiny output that takes two seconds to calculate shows a spinner, or it shows nothing and then jumps into place. So I looked for a skeleton package for Shiny.
What I found gave me spinners and overlays. They are good packages, and a spinner does one job well: it tells the user that something happens. But that is all it says. It does not say what is coming, or where.
I did not find a package that gives an output a placeholder in the shape of its content. So I decided to write one.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
section: The idea: the output already knows its shape
text:
The idea: the output already knows its shape
The first design question was the most important one. Where does the shape come from?
I did not want users to draw their skeletons by hand. A skeleton that you have to describe for each output is work, and work means that nobody does it. But a Shiny output already says a lot about what it will show. plotOutput() will show a chart. DT::DTOutput() will show a DT table, with its search box and its pages. textOutput() will show some lines of text.
So bones reads the output that you give it, and picks the shape from it:
library(shiny)
library(bones)

ui <- fluidPage(
  withBones(plotOutput("chart")),
  withBones(DT::DTOutput("patients"), rows = 10)
)
The chart gets columns on an axis. The DT table gets the “Show entries” control, the search box, ten rows and the page buttons. A gt table gets a title, a spanner and a source note. A leaflet map gets tiles, roads and pins. And if you do not want to wrap each output, one call wraps them all:
ui <- bones_auto(fluidPage(
  plotOutput("chart"),
  tableOutput("results")
))
That part was fun. The grey boxes themselves were the easy part. The hard part was everything around them.


A short recreation of what this post describes, made in a browser.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
Problem one: the second load
A skeleton is right for the first load. The page is empty, and the user waits for the first answer.
But a dashboard calculates again and again. The user changes a filter, and the chart calculates again. The obvious answer is to show the skeleton each time. It is the wrong answer.
When the chart calculates again, the user is often in the middle of reading it. The old chart is still an answer. It is a slightly old answer, and a better one comes a moment later. Grey boxes in its place remove information that the user was reading.
So bones shows the skeleton on the first load only. When an output calculates again, the old content stays on the screen, dimmed. The user can still read it, and can see that it is out of date.
There was a second part to this. When several outputs use one slow reactive, Shiny calculates them one after the other. If each output dims only when its own turn comes, the dimming crawls across the page one output at a time, and the outputs that wait look up to date when they are not. So bones dims all of them as soon as they are out of date.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
section: Problem two: a skeleton that flashes is worse than none
text:
Problem two: a skeleton that flashes is worse than none
Many loads are fast. If the data comes back in 100 ms, a skeleton that appears and disappears in 100 ms is not help. It is a flash, and the eye reads a flash as a fault.
So the skeleton waits. It appears only after 300 ms, so a fast load shows nothing at all. And when it has appeared, it stays for at least 500 ms, so a load that ends just after the delay does not flash it for one frame.
withBones(plotOutput("chart"), delay = 150, min_time = 400)
These two numbers made more difference to how the package feels than any of the shapes did.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
section: Problem three: the page must not move
text:
Problem three: the page must not move
A skeleton has a second job, and it is as important as the first. It keeps the space of the content, so the page does not jump when the content arrives.
This is easy when the output sets a height. plotOutput() is 400 px unless you say otherwise. It is harder for a table or a block of text, where the height depends on the data. bones estimates it from the number of rows or lines, and when the content arrives, the content sets the height. If the estimate was too tall, the space closes, and no gap stays under the content.
An estimate can still be wrong. So when the content arrives, the browser stores its real height. On the next visit, the placeholder keeps that height in place of the estimate, and from the second visit the page does not move at all.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
section: Problem four: display: none and renderPlot()
text:
Problem four: display: none and renderPlot()
This one is specific to Shiny, and I think it is the most useful thing in this post even if you never use bones.
The obvious way to hide the content under a skeleton is display: none. It does not work, and the reason is not obvious.
renderPlot() makes its image at the width of the output element. An element with display: none has a width of zero. So a plot that renders while it is hidden gets the wrong size. Shiny keeps that image, and the plot looks broken until something causes a new render.
bones hides the content with visibility: hidden in place of display: none, and puts the skeleton on top of it with absolute position. The output keeps its box, and only the paint is hidden. The plot always renders at the right width, because it always has one.
If you hide Shiny outputs in your own code, for tabs, for collapsed panels, for anything, this is worth remembering.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
What bones cannot know
There is one limit that I could not remove. plotOutput() says that a plot will be there. It does not say which plot. renderPlot() decides that later, on the server. So a plotOutput() gets the bar shape unless you say otherwise:
withBones(plotOutput("trend"), type = "line")
withBones(plotOutput("share"), type = "pie")
An interactive chart is different. A plotly, echarts4r or highcharter output sends a description of its series to the browser. So bones reads the kind of chart from the first value, and the next loads show that shape. With remember, the kind is stored in the browser, and the first skeleton of the next visit has the right shape too.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
The small things
A few decisions that are easy to miss:

The colours come from the theme of the page. A skeleton takes the tint of a branded bslib theme, and turns light in a dark theme, with no configuration.
Users who ask their system to reduce motion get no animation. A placeholder that moves is exactly what that setting is for.
The placeholder is hidden from screen readers. Shiny already tells them that an output is busy, and a second message would only repeat it.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
section: From a reel to a package
text:
From a reel to a package
The first commit of bones was on 23 September. The live demo on the package site runs in the browser with shinylive, so you can try every shape and option without installing anything.
A reel about how websites fool you with grey boxes turned into a package that does the same for Shiny. I do not think it is a trick, though. The wait is the same length. But a user who sees the shape of the answer waits in a better way.

title: A spinner says wait. A skeleton says what is coming.
text:
Try it
Update, 16 October 2026: bones is now on CRAN.
install.packages("bones")

shiny::runApp(system.file("examples/demo", package = "bones"))

Documentation: https://tenmeh.github.io/bones/
Live demo: https://tenmeh.github.io/bones/articles/live-demo.html
Source: https://github.com/tenmeh/bones

Issues and pull requests are welcome. I would especially like to hear about outputs that get the wrong shape, because each one is a shape that bones could learn.
